source1: Dept. of Ancient Near Eastern Art, 'Assyria, 1365-609 B.C.', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2004 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/assy/hd_assy.htm
source2: M. A. Dandamayev and E. A. Grantovskii, 'Assyria i. The Kingdom of Assyria and its Relations with Iran', Encyclopaedia Iranica II/8, 1987 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/assyria-i
notes: Neo-Assyrian start (Adad-nirari II, 911) is a modern periodisation; the same Assyrian kingdom continued at Assur (Iranica and Met narrate one state). 11th-10th c. losses to Aramaeans were external; internal unrest undocumented.

successor: Babylonia (Second Dynasty of Isin, Nebuchadnezzar I); later control of Susa unknown
source1: Francois Vallat, 'Elam i. The History of Elam', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-i
notes: Nebuchadnezzar I captured Susa c. 1110 BCE; Britannica says this ended Elamite power, then ~300 undocumented years. Vallat (Iranica): Susa lost only briefly, king fled to Anshan and returned. Later control unknown; sources disagree.

source2: Christopher Lightfoot, 'The Roman Empire (27 B.C.-393 A.D.)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2000 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/roem/hd_roem.htm
notes: Principate/Dominate is a periodisation: Diocletian (284) restored and reorganised the same imperial government at Rome. Q4: military anarchy of soldier-emperors 235-284 with Gallic and Palmyrene breakaways.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Syria: Hellenistic and Roman periods' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Syria/Hellenistic-and-Roman-periods
source2: Dept. of Ancient Near Eastern Art, 'The Seleucid Empire', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2004 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/sleu/hd_sleu.htm
notes: Listed capital Seleucia fell to Parthia 141 BCE; coded for Antioch, capital at end. Amid Seleucid civil wars Tigranes of Armenia seized Syria 83 BCE (one Britannica article says invited); Pompey annexed Syria 64-63 BCE.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Czechoslovak history: The late Middle Ages (1306-1526)' - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Czechoslovak-history/The-late-Middle-Ages-1306-1526
notes: Male Premyslid line ended with Wenceslas III's murder (1306); after a four-year throne struggle Bohemian magnates chose John of Luxembourg (husband of Premyslid Elizabeth) in 1310. Same kingdom. Q4: 'evil years' after 1278.

successor: Papal States - Early Modern Period II
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Papal States: The 15th century to the French Revolution' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Papal-States/The-15th-century-to-the-French-Revolution
notes: 1648 (Westphalia, condemned by Innocent X, pope 1644-55) is a period boundary; papal temporal rule continued until 1798. Q4: War of Castro 1641-44 with the Farnese, holders of the papal fief of Castro.

source2: Dept. of Asian Art, 'Tang Dynasty (618-907)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2001 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/tang/hd_tang.htm
notes: Tang army under Li Jing captured Illig (Jieli) Qaghan in 630; Britannica: 'In 630 Taizong occupied Mongolia' after internal strife. Rebel Xueyantuo vassals held the north under Tang suzerainty. Shiwei candidate is wrong.

successor: Carnatic Sultanate (Nawabs of Arcot; Chanda Sahib)
source1: District Administration Tiruchirappalli, Government of Tamil Nadu, 'History' - https://tiruchirappalli.nic.in/history/
notes: Nayak rule ended 1736 under regent Meenakshi amid succession war with Bangaru Tirumala; Chanda Sahib, son-in-law of the Arcot Nawab, gained Tiruchirappalli fort and took power. Scholarly sources not reachable; confidence low.

Paris Basin civitates (Parisii, Senones) are recorded by Caesar, so coded as polities, not S4. Caesar conquered Gaul 58-50 BCE (Lutetia and Alesia 52). Database 27 BCE reflects Augustan reorganisation.

source2: Suzan Yalman, 'The Mamluk Dynasty (1250-1517)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/maml/hd_maml.htm
notes: The sultan's own Bahri mamluks killed Turan Shah (1250) and took power: an internal coup. Ayyubid family disputes after 1238. Ayyubids lasted in Syria to 1260. Database Mamluk start (1260) is late.
